pair_convention.spot_explanation: NZD/CAD at 0.81123 means 1 NZD = 0.81123 CAD. A rising number means the New Zealand dollar is strengthening against the Canadian dollar; a falling number means the New Zealand dollar is weakening against the Canadian dollar. The price payload's spot of 0.81123 is dated 3 September 2026, two sessions after the 1 September valuation date, and every level, target, pip figure and distance-to-average in the report is computed against this spot.

executive_summary: NZD/CAD closed the gated weekday store at 0.81123 on 3 September 2026, meaning one New Zealand dollar bought 81.12 Canadian cents, and the pair has gone almost nowhere over six months (+0.90%) while losing 1.66% in the last month alone and 1.33% over twelve. That flat six-month line conceals a completed round trip: the pair made a rising sequence of higher highs and higher lows from the March low of 0.79236 up to a 52-week closing high of 0.82902 on 4 August, then rolled over into two lower highs and, on 2 September, its first lower low since April — a 113-pip single-session decline on the very day the RBNZ raised the OCR to 2.75% and the Bank of Canada held at 2.25%. That is the single most informative price fact in this report and it corroborates rather than contradicts the settled verdict: the bilateral policy differential widened to +50bp and the pair fell, because the widening was 94% priced on one leg and priced at a 3% hike probability on the other. The scored direction is Neutral on both horizons — tactical −0.0419, strategic −0.0454, conviction 2 each — and the composition matters more than the level: six of ten factors abstain tactically, while strategically a Bullish Policy & Rates contribution of +0.1152 is very nearly cancelled by a Bearish External Balance contribution of −0.1340 at a boosted 0.20 weight. The bilateral edge that does not exist in either standalone dossier is the netting: both dossiers are strategically bearish on their own currency (−0.1810 for NZD, −0.1029 for CAD), so the cross has no direction, and what remains is a dairy-versus-oil terms-of-trade transfer running against the base leg against a rate path running for it. Our one published disagreement with the verdict is not about direction but about asymmetry — the pair has just lost the 200-week average at 0.82175 for the first time (zero weeks since the last close above it) and made a lower low, so the distribution around a Neutral is skewed toward downside overshoot in a cross with no listed option and the thinnest base leg in the G10. Trade it small or not at all: 50bp of carry accrues 3.4 pips a month against a 47-pip ATR, and the probability-weighted expectation is −19 pips tactically and −27 pips strategically.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no pair-level PPP series for NZD/CAD, so relative valuation is taken from the two BIS real effective exchange rate readings for June 2026 — New Zealand at 101.12 against Canada at 95.71 — which places the New Zealand dollar approximately 5.4% to 5.7% rich to the Canadian dollar in real effective terms. Both dossiers derive this independently and arrive at consistent figures (+5.65% on the base dossier's convention, −5.35% on the quote dossier's). The base dossier's implied fair value on that construction is NZD/CAD 0.77342 against the current 0.81123, 378 pips below spot, sitting almost exactly on the 2-touch structural support band at 0.77080–0.77340 — a coincidence, not a forecast. Relative valuation reinforces the strategic negative tilt rather than generating a target, and what is priced at 0.81123 is a pair whose two legs are treated as broadly interchangeable commodity currencies despite the kiwi's commodities being soft rather than hard.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since early August has been a completed reversal in three phases. Through late July and the first week of August the pair rallied hard — from 0.81288 on 23 July to a 52-week closing high of 0.82902 on 4 August — on firm dairy auctions, a hawkish RBNZ repricing and a Canadian dollar absorbing tariff headlines. Phase two was an August erosion of two lower highs while Canada outperformed eight of ten G10 peers over the month. Phase three was the 2 September double decision, when the RBNZ hiked 25bp to 2.75% with a track little changed from May and the Bank of Canada held for a seventh time while flagging increased upside inflation risk — and the pair fell 113 pips, broke the 23 July low and lost the 200-week average. The dominant narrative is now relative rates versus relative terms of trade, with the market having just demonstrated it will not pay twice for a policy differential already discounted.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The bilateral policy differential is +50bp in favour of the New Zealand dollar post-2 September (OCR 2.75% against the Bank of Canada overnight target 2.25%). The gated payload's own policyDifferential of 0.25 predates the RBNZ hike and is disclosed as a vintage gap rather than a contradiction. Carry-to-vol on any of the available volatility comparators runs between roughly 7.8 and 8.6, thin relative to comparators elsewhere in the New Zealand dollar complex (AUD/NZD -40.84, NZD/JPY +20.66 on the same construction). The carry regime is assessed as not working and not relevant: fifty basis points on a mid-6% volatility estimate is economically trivial, neither leg funds the other, and NZD/CAD is a volatility and terms-of-trade trade rather than a carry trade. No quoted forward curve was obtainable; what exists is a CME futures-implied roll premium of -79.8bp annualised, roughly three times the +25bp differential prevailing at observation, implying a residual of 50-55bp of cross-currency basis and term effect that cannot be separated from the rate differential without an OIS curve.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The gated payload records the OCR at 2.50 per cent as of 2026-08-28 and the Bank of Canada overnight target at 2.25 per cent as of 2026-08-31, a bilateral policy differential of plus 25 basis points in favour of the New Zealand dollar. Both as-of dates precede the two 2 September decisions, which have since been published: the Reserve Bank raised the OCR 25 basis points to 2.75 per cent by consensus, and the Bank of Canada held at 2.25 per cent for a seventh consecutive decision. The bilateral differential is therefore plus 50 basis points and the widening is a completed fact rather than a forecast. Critically for a four-week view, that widening was almost fully discounted going in — the hike was 94 per cent priced on the New Zealand leg and the hold was priced at a 3 per cent hike probability with all 35 Reuters-polled economists forecasting no change on the Canadian leg — so the event delivered the differential without delivering a repricing. The pre-decision New Zealand two-year at 3.61 per cent against Canada at 3.01 per cent was already plus 60 basis points, ahead of the plus 25 basis point spot differential and roughly consistent with the move now delivered. Direction of travel over the next four weeks is flat on both legs: the Reserve Bank's republished track signals a pause on 28 October rather than a further move, and the Bank of Canada does not meet again until the same date. With no scheduled repricing event for either leg inside the tactical window, a thin plus 50 basis point differential that has already been paid for is a Neutral, not a directional input.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the bilateral differential is more likely to widen than narrow, but by a margin small enough and already discounted enough that confidence must stay below 50. The Reserve Bank's September track puts the average OCR at 2.81 per cent for the fourth quarter of 2026, a profile that maps precisely to a pause at the 28 October Monetary Policy Review and a 25 basis point increase to 3.00 per cent at the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement. Against a Bank of Canada that has now held seven consecutive times and which TD Economics expects to leave unchanged through 2027, that is a path to plus 75 basis points by 9 December. The offsetting risk is genuine and it strengthened on 2 September: the Bank of Canada explicitly stated that upside risks to its inflation forecast have increased with the Strait of Hormuz unresolved and refinery margins elevated, which partially validates the roughly 65 per cent probability of a 2026 Canadian hike embedded in Canadian OIS that the quote dossier intended to fade. If the Bank of Canada delivers one increase, the differential returns to plus 50 basis points and nothing has changed. The framing that matters is relative distance from neutral: the Reserve Bank estimates its neutral OCR at 3.0 to 3.5 per cent, so at 2.75 per cent heading to 3.00 per cent it is only reaching the bottom of neutral, while the Bank of Canada at 2.25 per cent against a 2.75 to 3.25 per cent neutral estimate remains 50 to 100 basis points accommodative and shows no intention of closing that gap. That is a mildly New Zealand dollar positive configuration. The countervailing structural fact is the plus 104 basis point ten-year differential, which is not a reward but compensation demanded of a small twin-deficit borrower with two of three agencies on negative outlook, set against a AAA sovereign running a current account surplus.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bullish across horizons for a purely calendrical reason. Inside four weeks both banks have just decided, both delivered exactly what was priced, and neither meets again until 28 October — there is no mechanism through which the differential can move. Over one to six months the Reserve Bank has published a dated, checkable path to 3.00 per cent by 9 December while the Bank of Canada has published no path at all and is expected by most of the street to stand still, so the differential widens on the central case. Confidence is nonetheless lower strategically (48 against 55) because a strategic stance is a forecast of two reaction functions rather than an observation of a resolved calendar, and because the Bank of Canada's 2 September acknowledgement of increased upside inflation risk makes the Canadian leg materially less inert than the quote dossier assumed. tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential looks large and is almost entirely an artefact of a shock both economies are absorbing simultaneously. New Zealand headline CPI is 4.06 per cent against Canada at 3.0 per cent, a 106 basis point gap, but the New Zealand overshoot rests on tradables at 4.9 per cent with petrol contributing 27.5 per cent of the annual rise, while the Canadian overshoot rests on gasoline up 25.7 per cent year on year. Strip energy out and the two economies are close to indistinguishable: the Reserve Bank's sectoral factor model core has been pinned at 2.7 per cent for four consecutive quarters, while Canada's CPI-trim is 1.9 per cent, CPI-median 2.0 per cent and CPI excluding gasoline 2.2 per cent — the Bank of Canada restated on 2 September that core measures remained close to 2 per cent in July. So the headline differential of 106 basis points shrinks to roughly 50 to 70 basis points on core and both banks are looking at the same Middle East energy shock. Growth and labour cut the other way and favour Canada: Canada printed 3.3 per cent annualised in the second quarter, a full percentage point above the Bank of Canada's own 2.5 per cent call, with unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4 per cent for a third consecutive month, while New Zealand's latest quarterly GDP is 0.8 per cent from the March quarter with unemployment at 5.6 per cent, a decade high, real wages falling 2.1 per cent and retail volumes negative for the first time in two years. Inside four weeks the data flow is dense on both legs and evenly signed, and the surprise ledgers point in opposite directions, with Canada running five beats to three misses in August against a New Zealand survey-versus-hard-data wedge that has not resolved. That is a genuine standoff.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both economies deteriorate and the honest bilateral conclusion is that they deteriorate at similar speed for different reasons. On the New Zealand side the energy base effect unwinds mechanically — Brent has fallen from 100.31 dollars on 24 July to 88.24 on 25 August and the Reserve Bank's own July revision cut the September-quarter CPI peak from 4.3 to 3.3 per cent — while unemployment at a decade high, retail volumes turning negative and house prices roughly 17 per cent below their November 2021 peak describe a domestic economy that cannot generate second-round inflation. Importantly, the September Monetary Policy Statement cuts against part of that reading: the Reserve Bank revised its 2027 inflation forecasts up on expectations of persistent domestic inflation, a majority of the Committee sees upside inflation risks, and it moderated its medium-term growth forecasts significantly on weaker consumption. On the Canadian side the deterioration is policy-imposed and dated: Statistics Canada's July advance estimate showed output flat at 0.0 per cent, measured before the 22 August Section 338 duties and before Canada's own 8 September counter-measures, against a Bank of Canada full-year 2026 growth projection of only 0.7 per cent that implies materially sub-trend outcomes in the second half after a 3.3 per cent second quarter. Roughly 2 million Canadian jobs are tied to goods exports to the United States and 5.2 per cent of them now carry 50 per cent duties, with an escalation to autos, trucks, parts and steel on 1 January 2027. Set the two against each other: New Zealand's drag is slow, domestic and disinflationary; Canada's is fast, external and simultaneously inflationary through cost pass-through and deflationary through demand destruction, which is why the Bank of Canada described tariff risks as pulling growth and inflation in opposite directions. Neither economy plausibly outgrows the other over the horizon and neither generates a clean relative inflation signal, so Neutral is a conclusion rather than a default.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: NZD/CAD is a moderate risk-on pair rather than a pure risk proxy, and the current regime gives it no directional information. The New Zealand dollar is the highest-beta risk currency in the G10, with the base dossier placing its correlation to AUD/USD at plus 0.85 to plus 0.95 and to the VIX at minus 0.3 to minus 0.5; the Canadian dollar carries roughly half that sensitivity, with USD/CAD to the S&P 500 at minus 0.2 to minus 0.3, because the deep US economic linkage anchors it. Long NZD/CAD is therefore a mild risk-on expression, with an approximate beta of 0.4 to 0.6 of an AUD/JPY-style position. The global backdrop is as supportive as it has been all year — the VIX at 14.43 to 14.51 having fallen more than 6 points in a month to its 2026 low, US high-yield option-adjusted spreads at 263 basis points tightened 21 to 24 basis points on the month, investment grade at 79 basis points and the S&P 500 at record levels near 7,670 to 7,686. On its published beta that configuration should have lifted the high-beta leg materially, and it did not: the New Zealand dollar lost 1.04 per cent against the US dollar over twelve months while the broad dollar index itself fell 2.04 points in August. Its realised risk beta has collapsed and the relative-rates axis has overwhelmed it. On the Canadian side the risk channel has partially decoupled for a different reason — oil is rising on a supply constraint rather than a demand signal, which raises Canadian export revenue while suppressing the global growth impulse that normally accompanies risk-on. Two decoupled channels pointing in offsetting directions produce no tactical signal.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months a VIX at its 2026 low and high-yield spreads at 263 basis points are levels to fade rather than extrapolate, and the New Zealand dollar has decisively worse convexity to that fade than the Canadian dollar. The structural asymmetry is specific and documentable rather than stylistic. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand holds no standing US dollar swap line with the Federal Reserve while the Bank of Canada does, and the Canadian line has not needed to be drawn. New Zealand must import capital continuously to fund a current account deficit of 3.6 per cent of GDP against a net international investment position of minus 42.8 per cent and net external debt of 49.0 per cent; Canada has just posted its largest current account surplus in twenty-one years and funded its capital account with a record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of government bonds in the second quarter. New Zealand dollar market depth is roughly 2 per cent of global turnover with 88,964 contracts of futures open interest, so positions are hard to exit in stress and the pair gaps outside Australasian and London hours; Canadian dollar futures open interest is 329,544 contracts and Canadian banks are deeply integrated with the US financial system. In a risk-off episode NZD/CAD falls through both the beta channel and the funding channel simultaneously, and it does so in a market with no shock absorber. The transmission is not hypothetical: over the past twelve months the New Zealand dollar has been the shock absorber within its own regional complex, losing 8.0 per cent to the Australian dollar, while the Canadian dollar outperformed eight of ten peers over the past month. Against this, the constructive case is real — credit spreads are tightening rather than merely tight, the AI capital expenditure cycle is intact and the Federal Reserve balance sheet has resumed expanding — which is why confidence sits at 55 rather than higher.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bearish because the tactical horizon trades the level of risk appetite while the strategic horizon trades the distribution around it. At a 2026-low VIX with high-yield at 263 basis points, the level is nominally supportive of the higher-beta leg and empirically has delivered nothing to it, which is a Neutral. Over one to six months the same levels are extremes from which outcomes skew toward deterioration, and the structural differences between the two legs — swap line, external funding need and market depth — convert that skew into a clean directional negative for the cross. Nothing about either currency changes between the windows; only which moment of the distribution is being priced.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Speculative money is short both legs of this cross, which is exactly the configuration in which a pair-level positioning signal collapses. As of the 25 August report date, leveraged funds were net short 31,994 New Zealand dollar contracts against total open interest of 88,964, while the combined Canadian dollar speculative short — leveraged funds at minus 72,092 and asset managers at minus 58,943 — stood at 131,035 contracts against open interest of 329,544. Normalised for market size those shorts are startlingly similar: approximately 36 per cent of open interest on the New Zealand leg against approximately 40 per cent on the Canadian leg. A crowded short in the base and a crowded short in the quote very largely cancel at the cross level, and the residual signal is the difference in flow direction, which is genuinely two-sided. The Canadian short is actively covering — 65,515 contracts, a third of the position, were bought back in the fortnight to 25 August with asset managers cutting from minus 108,343 to minus 58,943, and open interest fell 8.4 per cent on the week, the signature of liquidation rather than accumulation. The New Zealand short is being added to — leveraged funds put on a further 5,188 contracts in the week to 25 August into the Monetary Policy Statement. That flow differential is Canadian dollar positive and New Zealand dollar negative. Against it, the New Zealand short was running into a 94 per cent priced hike where the track was the only unknown, and the Canadian squeeze has a third of its fuel already burned. Confidence is capped at 48 because the New Zealand figures carry an unresolved data conflict: the legacy non-commercial series shows minus 14,200 for the same report date, disagreeing with the Traders in Financial Futures series on both level and direction, and no 25-delta risk reversal exists on either the New Zealand dollar or this cross to corroborate.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Positioning carries almost no information at a one-to-six-month horizon in either of these markets and the honest bilateral stance is Neutral at low confidence. The half-life of both books is far shorter than the window: the New Zealand dollar asset-manager category swung 25,889 contracts in a single week, equal to 29 per cent of total open interest, and the Canadian combined speculative net moved 65,515 contracts in a fortnight. Whatever either book looks like today tells you very little about February. What does survive the horizon is a structural asymmetry in absorptive capacity rather than in direction. Canadian dollar futures open interest of 329,544 contracts with dealers warehousing 124,930 of net length means the Canadian leg has a genuine shock absorber; New Zealand dollar open interest of 88,964 is roughly 2 per cent of the euro's and has none, so sustained directional flow in the New Zealand leg moves spot rather than open interest. That converts any strategic move in NZD/CAD into one that overshoots on the New Zealand side. Two unmeasured channels sit outside the futures data and pull in opposite directions: Japanese retail margin accounts hold significant New Zealand dollar carry exposure through NZD/JPY that would unwind on further Bank of Japan normalisation from 1.00 per cent against 1.8 per cent core, and Canadian pension funds run large global hedging programmes that generate mechanical Canadian dollar demand when foreign asset values rise, which they have with the S&P 500 up roughly 16 per cent year to date. Neither is observable in the weekly reports and neither is directionally reliable enough to score.

strategic.what_is_priced: Nothing durable is priced. Both futures books will look materially different within a month regardless of what the cross does, and the only strategically meaningful positioning fact is that the New Zealand leg has no absorber while the Canadian leg does — an asymmetry about the shape of a move rather than its direction.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Neutral, with confidence falling from 48 to 45. The tactical Neutral is a genuine standoff: two crowded shorts at near-identical shares of open interest with flows running in opposite directions. The strategic Neutral is an admission that positioning half-life is shorter than the window — the New Zealand asset-manager book alone turned over 29 per cent of open interest in a single week. Confidence is lower strategically because even the structural observation that survives, the absorptive-capacity gap between an 88,964-contract market and a 329,544-contract one, speaks to the violence of a move rather than to its sign.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Specs are short both legs at approximately 36% (NZD) and approximately 40% (CAD) of their respective open interest, so the cross-level implication is close to zero. The marginal flow is Canadian dollar positive — a third of the Canadian short covered in a fortnight against a New Zealand short still being added to.
tactical.unwind_trigger: For the base leg, an OCR track above the May profile — which did not arrive on 2 September, the September track being little changed and signalling a pause in October, so this trigger has now failed. For the quote leg, a soft Federal Reserve outcome on 16 September or confirmation on 20 October that Canadian core inflation is broadening, either of which would force the remaining 131,035-contract Canadian short into a dealer book already long 124,930 and unwilling to add.
tactical.historical_analogue: The base dossier records a legacy New Zealand dollar net short of 47,700 contracts on 31 July, roughly a third larger than today, after which the currency managed only plus 0.48% against the dollar in a month — a short base that size failing to generate a rally is evidence the selling was fundamental rather than speculative. On the Canadian leg the speculative short reached comparable extremes in the early-2025 tariff cycle and took roughly five months to normalise, with USD/CAD trading a 700-pip range rather than trending.
tactical.contrarian_case: The case against reading either short as fuel is that both crowds may simply be right. The New Zealand dollar carries a 3.6% of GDP external deficit, a dominant export down 11.3% year on year and two agencies on negative outlook; the Canadian dollar carries a permanent 50% tariff regime with no expiry and negative carry against the dollar. When two crowds are short two currencies for two coherent and unrelated reasons, the cross has no squeeze — it has two independent slow bleeds that happen to net out. The 2 September failure of the hawkish-track catalyst on the base leg is the specific evidence that the New Zealand squeeze thesis has already been tested and did not fire.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Residual stocks of minus 31,994 (NZD) and minus 131,035 (CAD) contracts are cushions under each leg rather than catalysts, and because they exist on both legs they cushion the cross in both directions. The only durable asymmetry is that the Canadian cushion sits in a market 3.7 times deeper.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A restart of formal US-Canada negotiations after the 3 November midterms would repricie the Canadian tariff premium in a single move and drive NZD/CAD sharply lower; conversely, delivery of the RBNZ's 9 December hike to 3.00% alongside a Bank of Canada that has still not moved would validate the base leg's differential and lift the cross. Both are dated and neither is priced.
strategic.historical_analogue: Both dossiers describe the same pattern from opposite sides — crowded shorts in small commodity currencies that resolve by range expansion rather than trend. The New Zealand dollar spent six months producing 15 pips against the US dollar with a large short base in place; USD/CAD spent five months in a 700-pip range unwinding a comparable Canadian short. The analogue for the cross is therefore range resolution rather than a directional squeeze.
strategic.contrarian_case: The strategic contrarian risk to any directional view here is that the two shorts unwind at different speeds rather than together. If the Canadian short keeps covering into the 28 October Monetary Policy Report and the New Zealand short is still being added to, the cross grinds lower on flow alone without any change in the fundamental differential — a mechanical move that would look like a fundamental verdict and would not be one. That is the specific reason positioning is scored Neutral here rather than being allowed to tilt the score: it is the factor most capable of producing a price move that means nothing.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Commodity-versus-commodity pair. NZD/CAD is the cleanest dairy-versus-oil terms-of-trade axis in the G10 and the base dossier names it as such explicitly; the framework's +0.03-0.05 adjustment pattern applies directly. Strategically stronger still because BoP flows accumulate — a 3.6%-of-GDP deficit funded from abroad against a 1.1%-of-GDP quarterly surplus is a six-month constraint, and the EIA expects the Hormuz supply disruption driving the oil leg to persist to end-2027. This is the one factor on which two independently produced dossiers point the same way for this cross with high confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest directional factor in the pair on both horizons and it points down. The commodity configuration is the worst available to NZD/CAD: oil is high and being sustained by a supply constraint while dairy has stopped falling but is not paying. Brent stood at 90.14 dollars and WTI at 85.45 on 31 August, both up more than 2.3 per cent on the session, and the Bank of Canada confirmed on 2 September that still-high oil prices and elevated refined-product margins persist with little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz — the US diesel crack exceeded 100 dollars a barrel for the first time. Canada is a net energy exporter and energy is its largest export category; New Zealand is a net energy importer for which the same move is a direct terms-of-trade tax, which is precisely why petrol at plus 27.5 per cent has driven New Zealand headline CPI to 4.1 per cent while worsening its external accounts. Dairy, the offsetting leg, has printed four consecutive positive GlobalDairyTrade auctions after the 4.9 per cent collapse of 7 July, but whole milk powder was down 0.1 per cent at 3,585 dollars at Event 411 on 1 September, still below its 3,706-dollar level of 2 June, cheddar fell 6.6 per cent, and the ANZ World Commodity Price Index fell 3.9 per cent in July with the dairy sub-index down 6.5 per cent on the month and 11.3 per cent on the year. The recent flow data reinforce the direction: New Zealand's July merchandise trade balance came in at minus NZ$1.95bn against an expectation nearer minus 175 million, with the annual balance deteriorating NZ$1.49bn in a single month, while Canada's June goods surplus rose to C$3.9bn on record exports of C$77.5bn, a fifth consecutive monthly increase. Bilateral trade between the two is immaterial at NZ exports of US$0.7bn and imports of US$0.4bn, so the transmission is entirely through third-market commodity prices rather than through direct flows.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.20 applied weight this is the dominant strategic factor and it is the least ambiguous evidence in the analysis: a country running a current account deficit of 3.6 per cent of GDP whose dominant export is down 11.3 per cent year on year, against a country that has just printed its largest current account surplus in twenty-one years with its dominant export explicitly carved out of the tariff regime that defines its risk. New Zealand's current account improvement stalled three quarters ago and the composition is structural, with a primary income deficit of NZ$3.3bn a quarter against a goods deficit of only NZ$1.1bn, generated by a net international investment position of minus 42.8 per cent of GDP. Dairy is roughly 30 per cent of merchandise exports, Fonterra cut its 2026/27 farmgate forecast from a 9.75-dollar midpoint to 9.25 on 13 July explicitly because reference-product prices had fallen 11 per cent on strong global supply, and the September-to-November spring supply peak arrives with whole milk powder already below its June level and a slowing Chinese buyer. Canada, by contrast, swung from a C$8.3bn deficit in the first quarter to a C$8.8bn surplus in the second, financed by a record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of government bonds, with the EIA projecting Brent averaging 87 dollars for 2026 and roughly 0.6 million barrels a day of Hormuz disruption persisting through the end of 2027. That is a multi-quarter, supply-side revenue transfer to a non-Gulf producer, and the tariff carve-out for energy, potash, fish and critical minerals means Canada's commodity complex trades on global prices rather than bilateral politics. Valuation reinforces rather than offsets: both dossiers independently place the New Zealand dollar rich to the Canadian dollar on relative BIS real effective exchange rates — a plus 5.65 per cent deviation on the base dossier's construction and minus 5.35 per cent on the quote dossier's — so the cheaper currency here is the one with the stronger external accounts.

Both errors point the same way for this cross and neither is small.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish on both horizons with confidence rising from 63 to 67 as the applied weight rises from 0.10 to 0.20. That is deliberate and mechanical: balance-of-payments flows accumulate, so six months of a 3.6 per cent-of-GDP deficit funded from abroad against a 1.1 per cent-of-GDP quarterly surplus is a real constraint where four weeks of it is not. Tactically the four-auction dairy stabilisation genuinely offsets part of the damage and caps confidence; strategically a 0.9 per cent index gain whose reference product is still below its June level offsets nothing against a Fonterra downgrade, a spring supply peak and a slowing dominant customer.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Dairy is roughly 30 per cent of merchandise exports with China the largest destination — GlobalDairyTrade index and whole milk powder are the reference prices, currently 3,585 dollars a tonne and below the 2 June level, with the ANZ dairy sub-index minus 11.3 per cent year on year and Fonterra's farmgate forecast cut to a 9.25 dollar midpoint. Secondary exposures are meat, forestry and aluminium (ANZ aluminium minus 8.2 per cent in July). New Zealand is a net energy importer, so oil enters through the import side as a terms-of-trade cost and a headline CPI shock, and LNG and refined fuel are pure negatives.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Crude oil and refined products are the largest export category by value, priced off WTI at 85.45 and Brent at 90.14 with a WCS-WTI heavy differential of roughly 12 dollars for 2026 capping realisation. Secondary exposures are natural gas (Henry Hub 2.94), potash, aluminium (benefiting from elevated global prices and European supply shortages), copper and lumber. Energy, potash, fish and critical minerals are all explicitly exempt from the US Section 338 duties, so Canada's commodity complex trades on global prices rather than bilateral politics.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the framework's direction rules leg by leg. Oil up: strongly positive for CAD (++) and negative for NZD as a net energy importer, so oil up is unambiguously bearish NZD/CAD — the two legs sit on opposite sides of the same move and the effects add rather than partially cancel. Dairy up: strongly positive for NZD (++) and mildly negative for Canada as a dairy importer with supply-managed domestic production, so dairy up is bullish NZD/CAD. Natural gas up: negative for NZD (imported energy input) and positive for CAD, bearish NZD/CAD. Aluminium and copper up: mildly positive for both legs, roughly neutral for the cross. The current configuration therefore stacks against the pair: Brent has been sustained above 88 to 90 dollars on a supply constraint the EIA expects to persist to end-2027, while dairy has stabilised at a level 11.3 per cent below a year ago that forced a Fonterra downgrade. Netting the two dominant legs: oil up strongly bearish plus dairy flat-to-weak mildly bearish equals a decisively bearish net commodity input for NZD/CAD on both horizons. Direct bilateral trade cannot offset this — at US$0.7bn of New Zealand exports and US$0.4bn of imports (IMF DOTS 2024) the direct channel is roughly a rounding error against either country's third-market commodity revenue. Canadian official figures corroborate the scale and composition: bilateral merchandise trade totalled C$1.6 billion in 2024, and the two economies sit inside the same CPTPP framework, establishing duty-free access — so there is no bilateral trade-policy risk premium in this cross at all, unlike the Canadian dollar's US-facing exposure.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent from approximately 90 to 99 dollars. Canadian export revenue and the current account both improve materially and the Canadian front end firms as the Bank of Canada's spillover concern intensifies — a double CAD positive. New Zealand's imported fuel bill and tradables inflation rise, terms-of-trade negative and only ambiguously rate-positive since the RBNZ has shown it will look through fuel. Net: bearish NZD/CAD, the largest single scenario risk to any long position in the cross, though the loonie's decaying oil beta (noted by CIBC) mutes but does not reverse the magnitude.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent from approximately 90 to 81 dollars. Canada loses the terms-of-trade support that produced its largest current account surplus since 2005 and Canadian headline CPI converges down toward core, removing the statistical basis for the ~65% 2026 Canadian hike pricing — a double CAD negative. New Zealand's tradables inflation falls faster, import-cost positive but also removes the fuel component justifying RBNZ tightening. Net: bullish NZD/CAD, but with less force than the symmetric oil-up case because the New Zealand benefit runs through an import bill while the Canadian loss runs through export revenue and the policy rate together.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil, not dairy. Dairy determines how much New Zealand earns; oil determines both how much Canada earns and what the Bank of Canada does next, and the two legs sit on opposite sides of every oil move. With roughly 0.6 million barrels a day of Strait of Hormuz disruption projected to persist to end-2027 and the Bank of Canada now explicitly citing elevated refinery margins as an upside inflation risk, oil is the single variable with the highest bilateral information content for this cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The communication-regime asymmetry between these two banks is the sharpest in the G10 and it favours the base leg, though by considerably less than the base dossier expected before 2 September. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is the only central bank in the developed world that publishes its own projected policy path, which makes the gap between that path and market pricing directly measurable. On 2 September it republished that track for the first time since May and delivered a hike by consensus, but the track was little changed: the average OCR for the fourth quarter of 2026 is 2.81 per cent against 2.84 per cent in May, a profile that maps arithmetically to a pause on 28 October and a hike to 3.00 per cent on 9 December, and the neutral OCR estimate is unchanged at 3.0 to 3.5 per cent. The hawkish surprise the base dossier anticipated — a published peak near 3.5 per cent — did not arrive, so the tactical guidance edge is a fraction of what it was framed to be. What did arrive is a committee with a majority seeing upside inflation risks and 2027 inflation forecasts revised up on persistent domestic inflation. On the Canadian side the Bank of Canada held for a seventh consecutive time with no published path at all and language that is deliberately two-sided — core measures close to 2 per cent and inflation excluding gasoline at 2.2 per cent on the dovish side, against an explicit statement that upside risks to its inflation forecast have increased with Hormuz unresolved. Net bilaterally: one bank has a published, dated, deliverable increase and the other has a conditional warning. That is a genuine but thin New Zealand dollar positive, hence Bullish at only 48.

RBNZ committee tilt: a majority sees upside inflation risks and 2027 inflation forecasts were revised up on persistent domestic inflation, while all members see downside risks to growth

Regime asymmetry: the RBNZ publishes a numeric path four times a year that can be compared with pricing; the Bank of Canada publishes no path and discloses an internal range of views
The base dossier's anticipated hawkish gap of 25-50bp did not materialise — the September track ratified May rather than lifting toward the 3.5% peak BNZ expected
tactical.what_is_priced: Both banks delivered what the market expected on 2 September and the higher-information release — the republished OCR track — came in essentially unchanged. What remains unpriced is only the relative credibility of a dated December hike against a conditional Canadian warning, which is a thin edge and is scored as one.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the guidance calendar is unusually informative because both banks decide on exactly the same two dates and the projection rounds alternate between the legs. On 28 October the Bank of Canada publishes a full Monetary Policy Report — its first fresh forecast round since July — while the Reserve Bank publishes only a Monetary Policy Review with no new track and has pre-signalled a pause. October is therefore a Canadian-dominant event, and it is genuinely two-sided: the Bank must mark down growth for the tariff shock while marking up its assessment of energy inflation risk. On 9 December the roles reverse: the Reserve Bank publishes a new Monetary Policy Statement with a fresh track and, on its own September projection, delivers a 25 basis point increase to 3.00 per cent, while the Bank of Canada issues a bare statement with no forecast. The sequencing is what tilts the factor: the ambiguous, Canadian-dominant round arrives first and the base-leg round with a delivered hike arrives second. Credibility cuts both ways and that is why confidence stays at 45. The Reserve Bank's transparency is real, but its track has been wrong twice this year, being overtaken by the July off-cycle hike within six weeks and requiring a 100 basis point downward revision to the September-quarter CPI peak inside eight weeks. The Bank of Canada's reaction function is public and highly credible but produces no comparable number, and its own Market Participants Survey median sits one to two quarters behind the roughly 65 per cent probability of a 2026 hike embedded in Canadian OIS — a wedge that would ordinarily favour this cross, except that the Bank's own 2 September acknowledgement of increased upside inflation risk has made it harder to fade.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices the RBNZ track as informative and the Bank of Canada as data-dependent, and prices a 2026 Canadian hike at roughly 65 per cent against the Bank's own survey median of March 2027. The unpriced element is the sequencing — an ambiguous Canadian forecast round on 28 October ahead of a delivered New Zealand hike on 9 December — and it is worth only a thin positive tilt to the cross.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bullish and both are held at low confidence, 48 tactical and 45 strategic. The stance does not change because the same structural fact drives it at both lengths: one bank publishes a numeric, dated, checkable path and the other publishes a conditional warning, and the path currently points up. Confidence is marginally lower strategically because the 28 October Canadian Monetary Policy Report is a genuine two-sided event on the quote leg and because the RBNZ's own track has already been overtaken by events twice this year, so a December hike published in September is a forecast rather than a commitment.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The four weeks in front of the valuation date carry materially more unpriced binary risk on the Canadian leg than on the New Zealand leg, which tilts the cross up. On 8 September Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect on approximately US$20bn of US imports at rates of 15 to 50 per cent covering steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics and motorcycles — and the product-level list had not been published as of the valuation date, so the market cannot have priced its composition. That follows the 22 August imposition of 50 per cent US duties under Section 338 across 554 tariff lines, the first presidential use of that authority since 1949, applied regardless of USMCA preference and carrying no expiry, with USTR confirming no new talks are planned. The Bank of Canada acknowledged both situations as fluid on 2 September. New Zealand's tactical calendar by contrast contains no binary political event until the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update on 29 September, at the very edge of the window, and its central bank decision has already resolved as priced. The important qualification, and the reason confidence is only 52, is that the tariff shock is not unambiguously Canadian dollar negative: the Bank of Canada explicitly framed the counter-tariffs as raising costs for businesses and potentially feeding into consumer prices, which is rate-supportive for the Canadian dollar even as it is growth-negative. A shock that raises both the inflation risk premium and the growth risk premium in the quote currency does not transmit cleanly to the cross. The common exogenous factor — the Middle East conflict and the contested Strait of Hormuz — reaches the two legs through opposite signs and is scored in Factor 5 rather than here.

tactical.what_is_priced: The date and headline value of the 8 September Canadian retaliation are known and its sector composition is not, and no option market for this cross exists to price any of it. The relative event asymmetry favours the base leg over four weeks, but the two-sided nature of a cost-raising tariff shock in the quote currency keeps the tilt modest.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both currencies carry identifiable political risk and Canada's is larger, dated and structurally unresolvable, which tilts the cross up. On the Canadian side, Section 338 permits proclamation-only tariffs with no investigation, no hearing and no time limit, so the duties remain until a future presidential proclamation removes them; Ottawa's own assessment is that no substantive talks resume before the 3 November midterms, Prime Minister Carney has committed support to affected industries beyond the life of the current US administration, and the escalation to 50 per cent on cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel is already announced for 1 January 2027. The USMCA architecture that would normally constrain this has been dismantled, with the mandatory review triggered on 1 July 2026 and US-Mexico talks proceeding on a separate track with Canada absent. The only dated circuit-breaker is the midterms, and its mechanism is indirect and slow. On the New Zealand side the risks are a general election expected in November on a three-year cycle, the 29 September Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update landing in front of two agencies already on negative outlook, and roughly twelve fortnightly dairy auctions with a tail exposure to any disruption of the China-New Zealand dairy relationship, estimated at a 5 to 8 per cent probability with a greater-than-3 per cent currency impact. Weighed against each other, a permanent and escalating trade rupture with a dominant customer outranks a routine democratic cycle plus a rating-outlook risk. The qualification that caps confidence at 54 is the same as tactically: the Canadian shock is inflationary as well as contractionary, so a portion of its severity leaks into support for the Canadian front end rather than into currency weakness.

strategic.what_is_priced: Neither leg carries any observable event premium — no option market exists on this cross and the Canadian six-month 25-delta risk reversal is minus 0.030%, symmetric pricing for an asymmetric dated escalation. The relative asymmetry favours the base leg, but a tariff regime that raises Canadian consumer prices as well as destroying Canadian demand does not translate one-for-one into a weaker Canadian dollar.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish on both horizons with confidence rising marginally from 52 to 54. The tactical case rests on a single bounded uncertainty — the unpublished composition of the 8 September Canadian retaliation list — that resolves quickly. The strategic case rests on the absence of any mechanism to end the regime at all, compounded by a dated escalation on 1 January 2027, against a New Zealand calendar containing only a routine election and a rating-outlook risk. Duration rather than magnitude is what strengthens the factor at the longer horizon, and the offsetting fact at both lengths is that a cost-raising tariff shock supports the quote currency's front end even as it damages its economy.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Neither sovereign will move this cross inside four weeks and there is a real ratings differential sitting behind that Neutral. Canada is rated AAA by Standard and Poor's, Aaa by Moody's and AAA by DBRS with AA+ from Fitch, one of only two AAA-rated G7 sovereigns, and no agency carries a negative outlook. New Zealand is AA+ foreign currency and AAA local currency from Standard and Poor's on a stable outlook, but Moody's placed its Aaa rating on negative outlook on 22 April 2026 and Fitch revised its AA+ outlook to negative on 20 March 2026 — two of three agencies negative. On the underlying numbers both are conservative and both are currently running better than forecast: New Zealand net core Crown debt is 41.3 per cent of GDP in the eleven months to 31 May, NZ$2.8bn better than budget, with the OBEGALx deficit NZ$3.0bn ahead of plan, while Canada's budget balance printed plus 0.99 at the 28 August release against a minus 0.31 prior and its 2025-26 deficit was revised down to C$66.9bn. Neither has an auction problem — New Zealand ten-year yields are clearing at 4.74 per cent without stress and Canada attracted a record C$80.8bn of foreign government bond purchases in the second quarter. The strategic risk is not a funding crisis — swap usage of US$121m and a fourteen basis point SOFR distribution say the convergence is orderly — but the fact that any sustained dollar firming or any episode of reserve scarcity is transmitted to NZD/CAD as base-leg weakness. tactical.rationale: At tactical weights this is a standoff, and it became one on 2 September. The two heaviest factors, Policy and Rates at 0.24 and Inflation and Growth at 0.18, together carry 42 per cent of the weight and both score zero. Policy and Rates is Neutral because the differential widening that the base dossier built its tactical case on has been delivered and was priced: the Reserve Bank hiked 25 basis points to 2.75 per cent by consensus and the Bank of Canada held at 2.25 per cent for a seventh time, taking the bilateral gap to plus 50 basis points against a New Zealand two-year that was already trading 60 basis points through Canada. The higher-information half of that event, the republished OCR track, came in essentially unchanged from May at a 2.81 per cent fourth-quarter average and signalled a pause on 28 October, so the hawkish surprise the base dossier expected did not arrive. Inflation and Growth is Neutral because both currencies are absorbing the same shock: New Zealand headline CPI of 4.06 per cent on petrol up 27.5 per cent against Canadian headline of 3.0 per cent on gasoline up 25.7 per cent, with core at 2.7 per cent and 1.9 to 2.0 per cent respectively, so a 106 basis point headline gap collapses to 70 or 80 on core and Canada holds the better growth and labour momentum. The two dossiers therefore conflict less than their headline stances suggest — the base dossier is tactically Bullish New Zealand dollar at plus 0.2230 and the quote dossier tactically Neutral Canadian dollar at plus 0.0012, but the base dossier's edge was specifically the OCR track and that edge has now been tested and failed. What is left is four factors where the legs genuinely differ, and they nearly cancel. Against the pair: the terms-of-trade configuration is the worst available to it, with Brent sustained above 90 dollars on a supply constraint the Bank of Canada itself confirmed on 2 September while dairy has stabilised 11.3 per cent below a year ago and forced a Fonterra downgrade, plus a 16 September FOMC at a 58 per cent hike probability that hits a currency with no Federal Reserve swap line far harder than one that has a standing line. For the pair: a central bank that publishes a dated path to 3.00 per cent against one that publishes only a conditional warning, and a Canadian trade rupture with no expiry and an unpublished retaliation list taking effect 8 September. The path of least resistance over four weeks is therefore sideways with a marginal downward tilt, and the dated catalysts are unusually dense and unusually evenly signed. Conviction is 2 because the offsetting forces are individually well evidenced and specific but the score gives almost no direction to trade, and because the single factor that would break the standoff — the terms-of-trade axis — is the one whose two 3 September prints are unknowable in advance.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the pair resolves into two large, well-evidenced forces pointing in opposite directions with almost equal weight, and the honest verdict is that they cancel. The bullish force is relative policy. The Reserve Bank's September track puts the average OCR at 2.81 per cent in the fourth quarter, a profile mapping arithmetically to a pause on 28 October and a hike to 3.00 per cent on 9 December, against a Bank of Canada that has held seven consecutive times, publishes no path at all and which TD Economics expects to leave unchanged through 2027 — a path to plus 75 basis points from plus 50 today. Reinforcing it is a communication-regime asymmetry that is the sharpest in the G10, one bank publishing a dated numeric path and the other a conditional warning, with the projection rounds usefully alternating between the legs on the two shared decision dates. The bearish force is external balance and terms of trade, and at a boosted 0.20 weight it is the single heaviest contribution. New Zealand runs a current account deficit of 3.6 per cent of GDP whose improvement stalled three quarters ago on a primary income deficit of NZ$3.3bn a quarter and a net international investment position of minus 42.8 per cent; its dominant export is roughly 30 per cent of merchandise trade, is down 11.3 per cent year on year, forced Fonterra to cut its farmgate midpoint from 9.75 to 9.25 dollars, and faces its spring supply peak with whole milk powder still below its June level and a slowing Chinese buyer. Canada has just printed a C$8.8bn current account surplus, the largest since 2005, achieved on goods trade, financed by a record C$80.8bn of foreign sovereign bond purchases, with energy explicitly carved out of the tariff regime and the EIA projecting Brent at 87 dollars for 2026 on roughly 0.6 million barrels a day of Hormuz disruption persisting to end-2027. Relative valuation agrees rather than offsets: both dossiers independently place the New Zealand dollar 5.4 to 5.7 per cent rich to the Canadian dollar on relative BIS real effective exchange rates, so the cheaper leg is also the one with the stronger external accounts. The two dossiers' standalone views are both strategically bearish on their own currency — minus 0.1810 for the New Zealand dollar and minus 0.1029 for the Canadian dollar — which is precisely why the cross nets close to zero, and the bilateral work is in deciding which deterioration is worse. The path of least resistance is a slow grind lower with the dated markers being Canadian CPI on 20 October, the 28 October Monetary Policy Report on the Canadian leg, the 3 November US midterms, a New Zealand election in November and the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement on the New Zealand leg. Conviction is 2: two forces of nearly identical magnitude leave a directional lean too small to press, and the heaviest single factor points against the net tilt.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Over one to six months NZD/CAD ranks in the lower half of the opportunity set in both complexes, for the specific reason that its two dominant factors cancel. Among New Zealand dollar crosses the base dossier's cleanest expression of its bearish strategic thesis is long AUD/NZD — 185 basis points of positive carry, 4.53 per cent realised volatility, a 12.77 per cent relative real effective exchange rate gap and a load-bearing two-year spread — and its secondary is short EUR/NZD; NZD/CAD ranks roughly sixth of nine because the New Zealand-negative external story is offset by a New Zealand-positive rate path that no other cross has to net out. Among Canadian dollar crosses the quote dossier's cleanest bearish Canadian dollar expression is short CAD/NOK, where the oil leg nets out, and its cleanest bullish is long CAD/CHF; NZD/CAD is again mid-pack. Where the pair does rank first is as a diagnostic: it is the purest dairy-versus-oil terms-of-trade read available in the G10 and the only cross whose two central banks decide on identical dates, so it is the best instrument in the complex for observing whether relative terms of trade or relative policy is the dominant driver, and the worst for expressing a strong view about either.

strategic.path_expectation: Expect a staircase, not a slide, and expect the first step to have already happened. The 2 September break beneath the 200-week average and the first lower low since April are the opening move, and the immediate sequel should be a month of consolidation between the 0.80800 pivot floor and the 0.81696 lower edge of the ten-touch band while the market waits for post-tariff Canadian activity data and the first clean read on New Zealand's September-quarter CPI. The second step is the 28 October Canadian Monetary Policy Report, which is the only genuinely two-sided projection event in the window — the Bank must mark down growth for tariffs while marking up energy inflation risk — and which is the more likely of the two shared dates to produce a range break. The third step is 9 December, when the RBNZ publishes a fresh track and, on its own September projection, delivers the hike to 3.00 per cent; if that arrives alongside a Bank of Canada still at 2.25 per cent it is the one identifiable event capable of pulling the pair back toward the 200-week average, which by then sits near 0.8235. Between those steps expect three to five weeks of sideways trade for every one week of directional move, because there is no forced-seller mechanism in a cross where both crowds are already short and neither dealer book is stretched. First, the base dossier's central tactical edge was a hawkish OCR track surprise, and the 2 September statement retired it — the track is little changed from May at a 2.81 per cent fourth-quarter average and signals a pause in October, so Policy and Rates is scored Neutral tactically where the base dossier scored it Bullish at 56. Second, the quote dossier's central strategic mispricing was fading the 2026 Canadian hike, and we weigh that fade less heavily because the Bank of Canada itself stated on 2 September that upside risks to its inflation forecast have increased with Hormuz unresolved. Third, and most importantly for the cross, we weight external balance and terms of trade at 0.20 strategically rather than 0.16, because NZD/CAD is the cleanest dairy-versus-oil axis in the G10 and the two legs sit on opposite sides of every oil move.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The verdict is Neutral, so the payoff is not directional. Its value is preventive: it declines to inherit the base dossier's tactical bullish conviction, whose specific catalyst has already been tested and failed, and it declines to inherit either dossier's strategic bearishness on the other's leg. Against the 0.8300 aggregator figure, a short held from 0.81123 to our 0.8070 six-month expectation earns 42 pips of spot plus roughly 32 pips of favourable futures roll, about 74 pips or 0.91 per cent — real but small.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the RBNZ delivers the 9 December hike to 3.00 per cent while the Bank of Canada is still on hold and Brent falls back below 80 dollars on a Hormuz reopening, the bullish rate factor stands while the bearish external factor collapses, and a Neutral verdict misses a move to 0.8290 or beyond — a 178-pip miss. Symmetrically, if the Bank of Canada hikes on 28 October while oil stays above 90 dollars and dairy fails at its spring supply peak, the bullish factor collapses while the bearish one strengthens, and the Neutral misses a move to 0.7950 — a 162-pip miss. Both are roughly 20-25 per cent outcomes, both are dated, and both are cheaply falsifiable at the 28 October and 9 December shared decision dates.

cross_horizon_consistency.tactical_stance: Neutral (breadth-driven: six of ten factors abstain, carrying 0.71 of applied weight)

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons derive to Neutral, at -0.0419 tactically and -0.0454 strategically, and both carry the same negative sign inside the band. But the alignment is superficial and the composition is entirely different, which matters for how the verdict should be used. The tactical Neutral is a Neutral of breadth: six of ten factors score zero because the two 2 September decisions delivered exactly what was priced on both legs, both economies are absorbing the same energy shock with core inflation near target, both currencies are crowded shorts at near-identical shares of open interest, and the chart was withheld from the scoring pass. The strategic Neutral is a Neutral of depth: only three factors score zero, carrying 0.19 of the weight, and the result comes from two large forces almost exactly cancelling. A Neutral produced by six abstentions and a Neutral produced by two high-conviction opposing views are different objects, and the second is the more fragile.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: 28 October, when the Bank of Canada publishes a Monetary Policy Report and the RBNZ publishes only a Review, and 9 December, when the roles reverse and the RBNZ publishes a new track alongside the hike its September projection implies
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the tactical Neutral as an instruction to wait and the strategic Neutral as an instruction to watch a single variable. Because the strategic result is two large opposing forces rather than an absence of signal, it resolves as soon as one of them moves: the pair turns directional if the terms-of-trade axis breaks. Any expression should be sized for a thin cross with no listed option and two bid-offer spreads, with execution and gap risk concentrated almost entirely in the base leg. On location: the price payload argues against chasing — a short at 0.81123 is entering 137 pips into a move already made, and a retest of the 0.81696-0.82486 ten-touch band from below is a materially better entry for the same thesis, with the 0.82175 200-week average as the natural stop reference.

catalysts.rationale: Resolved, and as priced on both legs: the RBNZ raised the OCR 25bp to 2.75 per cent by consensus and the Bank of Canada held at 2.25 per cent for a seventh consecutive decision, taking the bilateral differential to +50bp. The higher-information half of the event, the republished OCR track, came in little changed from May at a 2.81 per cent Q4 average and signalled a pause in October, so the hawkish surprise the base dossier's tactical case required did not materialise. Both decisions fall between the valuation date and the payload's spot date, and the pair fell 113 pips on the day, confirming the widening was fully discounted.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Overseas Trade Indexes (June quarter terms of trade) and ANZ World Commodity Price Index for August, alongside Canada's July merchandise trade balance
catalysts.rationale: The single most bilaterally informative day in the tactical window because both legs of the dairy-versus-oil axis print together. New Zealand's March-quarter terms of trade fell 2.0 per cent with export prices down 2.7 per cent against import prices down 0.7 per cent, and the July ANZ index fell 3.9 per cent with the dairy sub-index down 6.5 per cent on the month. Canada's July trade data predate the 22 August Section 338 duties entirely and carry an energy leg explicitly exempted from them, against a consensus of C$3.2bn that already assumes tariff damage.

catalysts.event: Canada Labour Force Survey (August) and Ivey PMI, plus CFTC Commitments of Traders for both legs
catalysts.rationale: Canadian employment consensus is approximately +15.8k after July's +75.1k, with unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4 per cent after three consecutive declines, which would support the quote leg. The same release carries the first positioning print covering the decision week for both currencies, with New Zealand leveraged funds net short 31,994 contracts and adding, against a Canadian combined speculative short of 131,035 contracts that has covered 33 per cent in a fortnight — the two positioning vectors point opposite ways, making the net bilateral read genuinely two-sided.

catalysts.event: Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect on approximately US$20bn of US goods at 15-50%
catalysts.rationale: An unpriced binary on the quote leg only: the product-level list covering steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics and motorcycles had not been published as of the valuation date, so the market cannot have discounted its composition. Dollar-for-dollar retaliation is proportionally heavier on an economy roughly one tenth the size of its counterpart. The transmission is partly offset because the Bank of Canada has framed counter-tariffs as cost-raising and potentially inflationary, which supports the Canadian front end even as it damages growth.

catalysts.event: Statistics Canada Consumer Price Index for August
catalysts.rationale: The most consequential quote-leg data point of the window and the direct test of the Bank of Canada's stated concern about oil spillover. Priors are headline 3.0 per cent, CPI-trim 1.9 per cent, CPI-median 2.0 per cent and CPI ex-gasoline 2.2 per cent for a third month. A rise in CPI-trim toward 2.2 per cent would validate the roughly 65 per cent probability of a 2026 Canadian hike and compress the +50bp differential in favour of the base leg; a slip below 1.9 per cent removes the statistical basis for that pricing.

The highest-frequency commodity event affecting either currency and the base leg's dominant terms-of-trade input. Event 411 on 1 September printed the index up 0.9 per cent, a fourth consecutive rise, but whole milk powder was down 0.1 per cent at 3,585 dollars and still below its 3,706-dollar level of 2 June, and cheddar fell 6.6 per cent. A fifth consecutive gain would establish a genuine floor and partially neutralise the heaviest strategic factor in this analysis; a fall greater than 5 per cent moves the base leg intraday.

catalysts.event: Federal Open Market Committee decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: The largest external risk to the cross inside the tactical window, and it transmits asymmetrically. A 58 per cent probability of a 25bp hike is priced, up from 36 per cent before Chair Warsh's 28 August Jackson Hole address. A firmer dollar hits both commodity currencies, but the base leg has no RBNZ swap line with the Federal Reserve where the Bank of Canada holds a standing one, must fund a 3.6 per cent-of-GDP external deficit continuously where Canada now runs a surplus, and trades in a market roughly a quarter as deep on futures open interest.

catalysts.event: Statistics New Zealand Balance of Payments and International Investment Position, June 2026 quarter
catalysts.rationale: The direct bilateral counterpart to Canada's 27 August print, and the comparison is the heart of the strategic case. Canada swung from a C$8.3bn deficit to a C$8.8bn surplus in the second quarter, its first since 2022 and largest since 2005. New Zealand's annual current account has been effectively flat for three quarters at approximately minus NZ$16bn, or 3.6 per cent of GDP, and with the July merchandise balance at minus NZ$1.95bn against an expectation near minus 175 million the June-quarter accounts are more likely to confirm the stall than the improvement.

catalysts.event: Statistics New Zealand Gross Domestic Product, June 2026 quarter
catalysts.rationale: The direct bilateral counterpart to Canada's 3.3 per cent annualised second quarter, which came in a full percentage point above the Bank of Canada's own forecast. New Zealand's March quarter grew 0.8 per cent, its strongest in nearly three years, and the survey evidence points higher while the hard data point lower with retail volumes down 0.5 per cent and unemployment at a decade-high 5.6 per cent. A print at or above the run rate narrows a growth differential that currently favours Canada.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Treasury Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (PREFU 2026)
catalysts.rationale: An independent Treasury view of the fiscal accounts published into an election campaign, and the first genuinely political event of the base-leg cycle with no Canadian counterpart inside the window. Budget 2026 has net core Crown debt rising from 41.9 per cent of GDP in FY25 to a 46.1 per cent peak in FY28 with the return to surplus placed in FY29, and it lands in front of two of three rating agencies already carrying negative outlooks — against a Canadian sovereign rated AAA by three agencies with no negative outlook at all.

catalysts.event: Statistics Canada CPI for September, and Statistics New Zealand September-quarter CPI in the same week
catalysts.rationale: Both legs' energy base effects unwind in the same window, which makes this the cleanest read on whether the 106bp headline inflation differential was ever anything other than a shared oil shock. On the Canadian side gasoline anniversaries out against a core running at 1.9-2.0 per cent; on the New Zealand side petrol contributed 27.5 per cent of the annual rise to 4.1 per cent and the RBNZ's July revision already cut the September-quarter peak to 3.3 per cent.

catalysts.event: RBNZ OCR decision with Monetary Policy Review AND Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report — both banks decide on the same day
catalysts.rationale: The projection round sits on the quote leg only, which makes this a Canadian-dominant event. The Bank of Canada publishes a full Monetary Policy Report, its first fresh forecast round since July; it must simultaneously mark down growth for the tariff shock and mark up energy inflation risk. The RBNZ publishes only a Monetary Policy Review with no new track and has already pre-signalled a pause. Genuinely two-sided for the cross and the most likely date for the strategic range to break.

The only dated circuit-breaker for the Canadian trade rupture inside the strategic horizon, and therefore the largest single upside risk to the quote leg. Ottawa's own assessment is that no substantive talks resume before this date, and Section 338 duties are removable by presidential proclamation with no statutory process, so a credible negotiation restart would repricie the entire Canadian tariff premium in a single move rather than gradually.

catalysts.event: New Zealand general election (expected November 2026 on the three-year cycle; exact polling day not confirmed and not asserted)
catalysts.rationale: The base leg's principal political event, following PREFU on 29 September and landing in front of two agencies already on negative outlook. New Zealand parties differ materially on housing, immigration and fiscal policy, and all three transmit to the currency. No election premium is observable because this cross has no listed option and the base leg's six-month surface carried only ordinary term-structure slope. Ambiguous in direction and material in variance.

catalysts.event: RBNZ OCR decision with Monetary Policy Statement and a new published track AND Bank of Canada decision — both banks decide on the same day
catalysts.rationale: The roles reverse from October: the projection round is now on the base leg. The RBNZ's own September track puts the Q4 average OCR at 2.81 per cent, mapping arithmetically to a 25bp increase to 3.00 per cent at this meeting following a pause in October, while the Bank of Canada issues a bare statement with no forecast and is expected by most of the street to remain at 2.25 per cent. Delivery would take the bilateral differential to +75bp, the widest of the horizon.

catalysts.event: United States tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel rise to 50%
catalysts.rationale: A dated, pre-announced escalation that extends the tariff regime well beyond the current 5.2 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States, striking the auto sector whose 27.0 per cent export surge helped drive Canada's second-quarter GDP beat. Section 338 carries no expiry, so the escalation persists until a presidential proclamation removes it. It sits just beyond the strategic window but is the event the horizon runs into, and nothing in either leg's volatility surface prices it.

assumptions: Price series as delivered: 130 data points covering 2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03, spot 0.81123 at spotDate 2026-09-03. Moving averages, the 200-week average, zones and the 52-week range are computed over the whole stored history (2007-12-24 to 2026-09-03, 4,879 weekday bars), not the 130 visible bars. weekendBarsDropped is 0, so all windows are true N-trading-day windows.

Spot-date gap, disclosed: valuation date is 1 September 2026 and the payload's spotDate is 3 September 2026, spanning both central bank decisions. All levels, targets, pips and distances are anchored to the payload spot of 0.81123; the two dossiers' vintage spots (0.81976, 0.82216) and a market-wrap-implied 0.8101 are disclosed as vendor/vintage dispersion of 22-109 pips and not substituted.

Settled direction carried verbatim: this is pass 2 of 2. All ten factor stances, confidences, weights, weighted contributions, net scores and rationales are reproduced unchanged from pass 1, scored without the price payload; the price data informs only market context, technicals, volatility, entries, targets, stops, sizing, scenarios and signposts. Factor 9 alone carries a labelled pass-2 addendum supplying the withheld chart without altering its stance or confidence.

Weight adjustments: Factor 5 up 0.04 on both horizons (commodity-versus-commodity pair, cleanest dairy-versus-oil axis in the G10) and Factor 10 down 0.04 on both horizons (non-USD cross); both within the framework's ±0.05 limit; weights sum to exactly 1.0000 on both horizons.

Implied volatility is an estimate, not a quote: NZD/CAD has no listed option. The payload's surface is derived from a variance identity fed a realised correlation of 0.6419 standing in for an unobservable implied one, flagged with a median 14.4% understatement across seventeen pairs. No IV percentile, risk reversal, butterfly, skew or barrier information exists for this cross.

Funding is a roll premium, not a rate differential: the -79.8bp annualised figure comes from a single CME calendar-spread observation (6C/6N, 31 August); by covered interest parity it embeds both the rate differential and cross-currency basis and the two cannot be separated without an OIS curve. Forward outrights are linear extrapolations of that one observation, not quoted prices.

Rate block vintage: the payload's policyDifferential of 0.25 predates the 2 September RBNZ hike; the post-decision +50bp differential is stated separately with its own source. The +104bp ten-year differential uses a monthly series roughly 94 days stale, breaching both freshness windows, and is used only as a like-for-like monthly comparison.

Bilateral trade taken verbatim from the supplied IMF DOTS 2024 block (NZ exports US$0.7bn, imports US$0.4bn); the reciprocal DOTS rows differ by the usual mirror-statistics margin and are not reconciled. The direct bilateral channel is immaterial against either economy's third-market commodity revenue, and CPTPP membership means no bilateral trade-policy risk premium exists in this cross.

Valuation methodology: no PPP series exists for this cross; relative valuation is derived from BIS REER readings for June 2026, an explicitly non-PPP proxy. Both dossiers flag the underlying BIS extract as cache-sourced and disagreeing with a direct BIS pull. The June reference period is roughly 63 days before the valuation date, marginally outside the strategic freshness window.

Consensus: no bank publishes an NZD/CAD forecast. A derived cross from the two dossiers' NZD/USD and USD/CAD clusters spans roughly 0.790 to 0.842 and is too wide to constitute a consensus. Pure-extrapolation forecast aggregator sites returned by search are excluded as a category error rather than treated as weak sources.

Other documented gaps: no sovereign CDS for either leg; no quoted three-month cross-currency basis for either leg; no option barrier or round-number dealer information for NZD/CAD; an unresolved conflict between the TFF (-31,994) and legacy non-commercial (-14,200) CFTC series for the New Zealand dollar on the same date; the New Zealand general election date is a placeholder inside an expected November window; the 15 September GDT date follows the published fortnightly cadence rather than a confirmed calendar entry.

Stance derivation: both net stances follow mechanically from the weighted scores per the framework threshold rule (≥+0.10 Bullish, ≤-0.10 Bearish, otherwise Neutral). At -0.0419 and -0.0454 both are Neutral; the negative tilt is expressed in prose rather than by relabelling either stance, and no confidence was tuned to move a score across a threshold.
